Indeed the University of Madras did give Ramanujan a scholarship in May 1913 for two years and, in 1914, Hardy brought Ramanujan to Trinity College, Cambridge, to begin an extraordinary collaboration.

Ramanujan was born in his grandmother's house in Erode, a small village about 400 km southwest of Madras (now Chennai). When Ramanujan was a year old his mother took him to the town of Kumbakonam, about 160 km nearer Madras.

However, the following year his scholarship was not renewed because Ramanujan devoted more and more of his time to mathematics and neglected his other subjects.

In the following years he worked on mathematics developing his own ideas without any help and without any real idea of the then current research topics other than that provided by Carr's book.
After publication of a brilliant research paper on Bernoulli numbers in 1911 in the Journal of the Indian Mathematical Society, he gained recognition for his work.
